content: The Aurum Institute received grants for several clinical trials. The Rifapentine and Moxifloxacin for Tuberculosis (Rifaquin) trial was funded with approximately €500,000, which expired in 2011. The REMoxTB trial received less than €200,000 and is ongoing. The Thibela TB trial was supported with US $32 million, which expired in 2012. The evaluation of the Xpert MTB/RIF diagnostic test was funded with US $13 million and is ongoing. The evaluation of TB/HIV integration received US $250,000, which expired in 2011. Dr. Raquel Duarte disclosed receiving payments from Pfizer, Abbott, and Janssen between 2011 and 2014 for delivering lectures on tuberculosis (TB) screening in patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases who were candidates for biological therapy. Dr. Diane Havlir declared receiving support grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for TB research. Dr. Christopher Lange disclosed receiving remuneration from Celltrion Korea in 2013 for consulting on the risk of TB associated with treatment using biosimilar TNF antagonists. Dr. Martina Sester declared receiving non-monetary support from Qiagen (formerly Cellestis) and Oxford Immunotec for investigator-initiated research studies, with free-of-charge provision of kits by these companies. She also received travel support from Qiagen to present data at scientific meetings and is a co-inventor of a patent application for an in vitro process to quickly determine a patient’s status regarding Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection (international patent number WO201113953/A1). Dr. Dalene von Delft disclosed receiving support from the Treatment Action Group (TAG) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) to give presentations at the International Union Against TB and Lung Diseases Conferences in 2012 and 2013. She also received support from Janssen Pharmaceuticals to attend the Leadership Summit on the Critical Path to TB Drug Regimens (CPTR) and from the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH)-AERAS to attend meetings. Dr. Dominik Zenner disclosed being a co-author of a systematic review on latent TB infection (LTBI) treatment and serving as the head of the TB screening unit in Public Health England, with a professional interest in the subject matter. The World Health Organization (WHO) issued a recommendation in 2011 for providing at least 36 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) to adults and adolescents living with HIV in resource-constrained settings with high TB and HIV prevalence. HIV infection is the strongest risk factor for developing TB disease in individuals with latent or new Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, with a 30-fold increased risk compared to those without HIV. TB accounts for more than a quarter of deaths among people living with HIV. IPT is a key intervention for TB prevention in this population. The 2011 WHO guidelines conditionally recommended 36 months of IPT as a proxy for lifelong or continuous treatment in high TB prevalence settings, based on unpublished studies at the time. The evidence has since been updated with published studies, necessitating a reassessment of the recommendation. The updated recommendation aims to provide IPT for 36 months to children and adults living with HIV, including pregnant women, those receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), and those who have completed TB treatment, in high TB and HIV prevalence settings. The recommendation is conditional due to the low quality of evidence, feasibility concerns, and potential adverse events. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials were conducted to assess the outcomes of continuous IPT versus six-month IPT. The evidence was reviewed by a WHO Guidelines Development Group, which included external experts, national TB program managers, academics, and representatives of patient groups and civil society. The updated recommendation emphasizes that adults and adolescents living with HIV in high TB incidence settings should receive at least 36 months of IPT, regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, history of TB treatment, or pregnancy. The recommendation is conditional and based on low-quality evidence. The benefits of longer-term IPT are greater in individuals with a positive tuberculin skin test (TST), and TST is encouraged when feasible. However, TST is not a prerequisite for IPT. Those with a negative TST should not receive 36 months of IPT. National authorities should define high TB incidence settings based on local epidemiology and transmission patterns. The systematic review identified three randomized controlled trials comparing continuous IPT with six-month IPT. The meta-analysis showed a significant reduction in active TB incidence with longer IPT, particularly in TST-positive individuals. Adverse events were not consistently reported, and adherence was inadequately defined in the studies. Observational studies also supported the benefits of 36 months of IPT but lacked data on side effects. The cost-effectiveness of continuous IPT is limited, with incremental costs reported for TB and death averted in TST-positive individuals. In conclusion, the WHO recommends 36 months of IPT for people living with HIV in high TB prevalence settings, with the potential for greater protective benefits in TST-positive individuals and those receiving ART. The recommendation is conditional due to the low quality of evidence and implementation considerations.
